title: 深入解析《注意力就是一切》：全面拆解论文并分阶段使用 PyTorch 实现
author: Herender Kumar
content:
I'm still pretty new to reading research papers, and "Attention Is All You Need" is the first one I've gone through line by line and then coded up myself. This post is the explanation I wanted while I was reading it. I wrote it for people like me: you can read Python, but you haven't spent much time with papers.

Start with this sentence from the Winograd Schema Challenge: "The trophy doesn't fit into the brown suitcase because it's too small." What does it refer to? Now swap the last word for large and read it again. Original example, item 2

Which object changed in your reading?

With small, the suitcase is the problem. With large, it's the trophy. Neither noun moved, but a word at the very end of the sentence changed how you read a word near the start. If you're translating into French, you run into this before you even reach the adjective, because the pronoun for la valise is elle and the pronoun for le trophée is il. Winograd schemas in translation

If I were translating that sentence, I'd want to read all of the English before picking a French pronoun. Thinking about it that way helped me understand the paper's architecture diagram, which has two halves. On the left, the encoder reads the source sentence and builds a description of each word in context. On the right, the decoder uses those descriptions, plus the French it has written so far, to pick the next word. During training the whole correct translation is already sitting there, so how does the decoder get to read every English word while the next French word stays hidden? It comes down to one line of Python, and we'll get to it.

If you know Python, you can run the small version at the end on a normal CPU. On your first read, I'd follow one word through the examples and the tensor shapes and skip the trigonometry for now. To try the code, copy the six Python blocks from Part 3 into a file called transformer.py, in order. All the papers and docs I used are listed at the very end.

Part 1: Things to know before the paper

1. Reading a tensor shape like a sentence

A token is a chunk of text with an integer ID. It can be a whole word, part of a word, or punctuation. An embedding is a row of numbers the model learns for that ID, and looking one up works a lot like indexing a Python list. The number for suitcase is only an address. Whatever the model learns about suitcases lives in the row at that address.

Now picture two shop receipts side by side, one with five items and one with three. If you type them into a spreadsheet with five slots per receipt, the second one ends up with two empty slots. We do the same thing with sentences so PyTorch can process several at once. A group of sentences processed together is a batch, and a special padding token, PAD, fills the empty positions. (I'll come back to these receipts when we get to masking.)

Say we have two sentences padded to five tokens. Their IDs have shape [2,5]. Look up each ID in a 512-dimensional embedding table and you get [2,5,512]. I read x[1,3] out loud as "second sentence, fourth token", and it gives you all 512 features for that token. A linear layer from 512 features to 64 works on each row separately and gives [2,5,64].

The letters in the code mean this: B is the number of sentence pairs, S and T are the source and decoder-input lengths, D is the number of features, and H is the number of heads. A V at the end of a logits shape is the vocabulary size. (Confusingly, the V in the attention equation is something else, a matrix of values.)

Two rules cover most of the shape checking you'll need to do.

  • In a matrix multiplication, the two inner dimensions have to match. For one head, Q with shape [T,dk] [T,d_k] times K⊤K^\top with shape [dk,S] [d_k,S] gives [T,S][T,S] . Entry (t,s)(t,s) compares target position t with source position s. If there are batch and head axes in front, PyTorch does the same multiplication separately for each pair of leading indices.
  • With broadcasting, an axis of size one gets reused along that axis. That's how a source mask of shape [B,1,1,S] works against scores of shape [B,H,T,S]. Each sentence gets its own allowed source keys, and every head and every target position in that sentence shares them.

2. Dot products and softmax

Take two short lists, [1,2][1,2] and [3,4][3,4] . Multiply the matching entries and add them up: 1×3+2×4=111\times3+2\times4=11 . That's a dot product, and attention uses it to score how well a query matches a candidate. Both the direction and the length of the vectors affect the score. A projection is a learned linear map that gets the features ready for that comparison.

Softmax turns a list of scores into shares that add up to one: raise e to each score and divide by the total, pj=esj/∑iesi p_j=e^{s_j}/\sum_i e^{s_i} . Then attention takes a weighted average of the values using those shares. That's all it is, a weighted average where the weights get recomputed for every query.

A small worked example, because it helped me: scores [log⁡3,0][\log 3,0] become [3,1][3,1] after exponentiating, and [0.75,0.25][0.75,0.25] after dividing by the sum. Give each candidate two features, [2,0][2,0] and [0,4][0,4] . The weighted result is [1.5,1][1.5,1] , and its second coordinate came entirely from the candidate with the lower score. Remember that when you get to weights @ v in the code.

3. Four PyTorch pieces you'll see everywhere

PyTorch piece What to know before reading the code
nn.Module You define layers in __init__ and the data flow in forward, then run it with model(x). Use nn.ModuleList for a variable number of layers so PyTorch registers their parameters with the model.
nn.Linear(in_features, out_features) Changes the last axis of any batch-first tensor. Its weight is stored with shape [out_features,in_features], which makes the weight tying in Phase 5 very simple.
nn.LayerNorm(D) Takes a mean and variance across the D features of each token on its own, then applies a learned scale and offset. Padding in one sentence can't change another token's normalization.
nn.Dropout(p) During training, randomly zeros individual activations and scales the survivors by 1/(1−p)1/(1-p) . model.eval() turns dropout off and torch.no_grad() stops gradient tracking. A repeatable inference test uses both.

4. Why recurrent networks were slow

Before Transformers, translation models were mostly RNNs, which read one word at a time. It's like working out a running bank balance from a statement: the balance after line 80 needs the balance after line 79, so nobody can start on line 80 early. An RNN writes this as ht=f( ht−1 ,xt) h_t=f(h_{t-1},x_t) , where ht−1 h_{t-1} is what it remembers from the previous step.

Training has a second problem. If a mistake on the last word should change how the network reads the first word, the correction has to travel backward through every step in between, and it can fade (or blow up) along the way. That's the vanishing gradient problem. LSTMs help with the fading, but they still wait for the previous step.

Self-attention connects any two allowed positions directly in one layer. Convolutions can run positions in parallel too, but they need several layers to reach distant words. The Transformer swapped all of that for one big matrix comparing every pair of positions.

Part 2: Walking through the paper

1. The overall architecture: who can read what?

Suppose the decoder has already written sur la ("on the"). Given the English source, how likely is rive ("bank" or "shore") as the next word? The model answers that question for every word, and multiplying the answers together gives the probability of the whole translation.

p(y1,…,yT∣x)= ∏t=1T p(yt∣ y<t ,x). p(y_1,\ldots,y_T\mid x)=\prod_{t=1}^T p(y_t\mid y_{<t},x).

Here x is the source sentence and y<t y_{<t} means "the target tokens before position t". In code it works out like this. After six encoder blocks, memory has one vector for each source position, and the vector for bank can now carry a hint from river. In each of the six decoder blocks, a target position can look back into that same encoder memory. After the last block the model gives a score, called a logit, to every possible next token. The logits have shape [B,T,V], so if you pick one sentence and one position you're left with V candidate scores.

Attention site Queries come from Keys and values come from Score shape
Encoder self-attention Current source states Same source states, all real positions [B,H,S,S]
Decoder self-attention Current target states Same target states, allowed prefix only [B,H,T,T]
Decoder cross-attention Decoder states after masked self-attention and Add & Norm Final encoder memory, all real source positions [B,H,T,S]

The catch with comparing every pair is the cost. For a sentence of length n, attention does work proportional to n2n^2 , so doubling the length gives you four times as many scores to store. Also, "parallel" only applies to training. When the model translates new text, it still has to produce one word before it can produce the next.

2. Embeddings and position: how does the encoder know word order?

If you give the encoder token embeddings alone, it can't tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog". Swapping two tokens just swaps the matching output rows, because each token still has the same set of partners to read. So the paper adds a fixed vector to each token's learned vector at position p:

xp=D E[ tokenp ]+PE(p),PE(p,2i)=sin⁡(pωi),PE(p,2i+1)=cos⁡(pωi),ωi=10000−2i/D. x_p=\sqrt{D}\,E[\mathrm{token}_p]+PE(p),\qquad PE(p,2i)=\sin(p\omega_i),\quad PE(p,2i+1)=\cos(p\omega_i),\quad \omega_i=10000^{-2i/D}.

The lookup says which token it is, and the fixed vector says where it sits. Adding them (instead of sticking them together) keeps the width at D, which the residual connections need. In my code each embedding coordinate starts small, around D−1/2D^{-1/2} , so multiplying by D \sqrt D brings it up to about the same size as the sine and cosine values. That starting scale is my choice; the paper doesn't say how they initialized the embeddings.

The way I finally understood the sines and cosines was a clock. A sine/cosine pair is like the tip of a clock hand: two coordinates that tell you where on the circle it is. Each pair in the position vector is a hand turning at a different speed. Moving one token forward barely moves the slow hands and moves the fast ones a lot, so between them they pin down the position.

Why both sine and cosine, though? This was the bit I had to read a few times, so skip it on a first read if you like. At a fixed speed, moving forward k positions is a rotation, and the trig identity sin⁡((p+k)ω)=sin⁡(pω)cos⁡(kω)+cos⁡(pω)sin⁡(kω)\sin((p+k)\omega)=\sin(p\omega)\cos(k\omega)+\cos(p\omega)\sin(k\omega) shows the coefficients only depend on k. In plain words, "three words later" looks the same wherever you are in the sentence, which seems like something a learned projection could pick up on. The authors tried learned positions too and got about the same results. They say they chose the sinusoids because they might work on sentences longer than the training ones, but as far as I can tell, this paper doesn't test that.

3. Scaled dot-product attention: what does a token pull in?

The query, key and value names clicked for me with a railway departure board. You walk up knowing where you're going (your query), you scan the destination column (the keys), and when you find your train you read off its platform (the value). A Transformer doesn't pick just one row; it takes a weighted mix of all of them. In the suitcase sentence, it can pull a bit from suitcase and a bit from small at the same time.

Attention⁡(Q,K,V)= softmax⁡keys ! ( QK⊤ dk ) V. \operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)= \operatorname{softmax}_{\mathrm{keys}}!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V.

I read that equation as three lines of Python. First comes scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(q.size(-1)). Each row of scores belongs to one query, and its columns say how well each key matched. Then weights = scores.softmax(dim=-1) turns each row into shares, and weights @ v mixes the values using those shares. So four decoder positions can each read all seven words of a source sentence and you still get exactly four outputs, one per query.

The only strange-looking number in that first line is dk \sqrt{d_k} . dk d_k is the number of features used for one match, so with 64 features we're adding up 64 products. If you assume each product is random noise with variance one, the variances add up to 64, so the total swings by about 8 in either direction. Dividing by 8 brings it back to around 1.

Why bother? Because softmax gets very sure of itself when scores are far apart. With a gap of 8 points, the winner gets basically all the weight (over 99.9%), and nudging its score does almost nothing, so the model barely learns. With a gap of 1, the winner gets roughly three quarters and the loser still gets a real share. (In calculus terms the slope is p(1−p)p(1-p) , which is close to zero in the first case and about 0.2 in the second.)

4. Multi-head attention: why eight heads?

Read the suitcase sentence again and ask two questions. Which things could it refer to? And which word tells you why one of them doesn't fit? For the first question, your eyes go back to trophy and suitcase. For the second, they jump ahead to small. Same sentence, different words, depending on the question.

One head gives each query one set of weights. With two heads, one could look at the nouns while the other looks at the adjective, and both results get passed on. That's a story about what heads could do, though. You'd have to inspect a trained model to know what its heads really learned.

headi =Attention⁡(QWiQ,KWiK,VWiV),MHA=Concat⁡( head1 ,…, headH )WO. \mathrm{head}_i=\operatorname{Attention}(QW_i^Q,KW_i^K,VW_i^V),\qquad \mathrm{MHA}=\operatorname{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1,\ldots,\mathrm{head}_H)W^O.

In the Base model, each of the eight heads projects all 512 input features down to 64. Stick the eight heads back together and you're back at 512, and WOW^O learns how to mix them. Because 8×64=5128\times64=512 , eight heads cost about the same arithmetic as one big head, though each head still needs memory for its own score matrix. The paper's appendix has attention pictures, including heads that seem to link the distant words in making ... more difficult. I'd treat those pictures as hints, not proof of what a head does.

5. Masking: two ways a decoder can cheat without you noticing

Back to the shorter receipt. To get its average item price, you divide the three prices by three. If you fill the two blank rows with zero prices and divide by five, you get a different (wrong) answer. Attention has a similar denominator. If three real tokens and two PAD tokens all get the same score, each real token gets one fifth of the weight, so even if PAD's values are zero, the real words end up with too little. A padding mask removes the empty rows before softmax, and each real token gets one third. We use the source padding mask inside the encoder and again when the decoder reads the encoder memory.

A causal mask handles a different problem. Take sur la rive and cover the label row in the table below with your hand. At position 2, only look at the decoder input up to that column. Which French words can you use to guess what comes next? <BOS> marks the beginning and <EOS> the end.

Decoder position 0 1 2 3
Decoder input <BOS> sur la rive
Label to predict sur la rive <EOS>

Uncover the prediction at position 2

You can read sur la, and you're trying to predict rive. Reading la in your own column is fine, because the labels are shifted one place. If you can see rive in the input to your right, you've uncovered one word too many. The whole English source is available the entire time.

The same rule as a matrix: rows are queries, columns are keys, and 1 means the query can read that key. 

             BOS  sur  la  rive
query BOS     1    0   0    0
query sur     1    1   0    0
query la      1    1   1    0
query rive    1    1   1    1

The diagonal is allowed because the inputs are shifted. If you feed in the unshifted labels, the answer sits at the same position and leaks through, including through the residual path. If you shift correctly but forget the causal mask, the answer is visible one position to the right. Training with the true previous tokens like this is called teacher forcing. When the model translates for real, those previous tokens come from what it has generated so far.

In the code, decoder self-attention uses causal & real_target_keys, and cross-attention uses only the source padding mask. Blocked scores get set to −∞-\infty before softmax, so they end up with zero weight. A padded query still produces an output, but its label is ignored in the loss, and nothing later ever reads it as a key.

6. Feed-forward networks, residual connections and LayerNorm

After attention, every token goes through the same small two-layer network on its own. That's what position-wise means: same weights, applied to each row separately. Attention has already mixed in information from the other tokens by this point.

FFN⁡(x)=ReLU⁡(xW1+b1)W2+b2. \operatorname{FFN}(x)=\operatorname{ReLU}(xW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2.

In Base, the first layer widens each token from 512 features to 2,048, ReLU zeroes out the negatives, and the second layer brings it back to 512 so it can be added to the original row. Without the ReLU in the middle, the two linear layers would collapse into one, which is a nice thing to check on paper if you've never done it.

Around every attention and FFN sub-layer F, the original Post-LN block computes LN⁡(x+Dropout⁡(F(x)))\operatorname{LN}(x+\operatorname{Dropout}(F(x))) . The residual sum keeps the old representation and adds a correction on top, and then LayerNorm rescales each token's features.

You can check LayerNorm by hand with three numbers. Say a token holds [2,4,6][2,4,6] and its sub-layer proposes an update of [1,0,−1][1,0,-1] , with dropout off. The sum is [3,4,5][3,4,5] . Its mean is 4, so LayerNorm first centers it to [−1,0,1][-1,0,1] , then divides by the standard deviation (plus a tiny epsilon), and finally applies its learned scale and offset. Every token gets its own separate calculation.

Most newer models use Pre-LN instead, x+Dropout⁡(F(LN⁡(x)))x+\operatorname{Dropout}(F(\operatorname{LN}(x))) , where the shortcut path skips the normalization. As far as I understand the later analysis (Xiong et al., linked at the end), this makes gradients better behaved early in training and is part of why the original Post-LN setup needed a warmup period. My ResidualConnection sticks with the 2017 Post-LN order.

7. Training, regularization and what the experiments showed

The loss measures how much probability the model gave to the correct next token, and a gradient says how the loss would change if you nudged a weight. The paper trains with Adam ( β1=0.9 \beta_1=0.9 , β2=0.98 \beta_2=0.98 , ϵ=10−9\epsilon=10^{-9} ) and this learning-rate schedule, where s counts steps from one and w=4000w=4000 is the number of warmup steps:

lr⁡(s)=D−1/2min⁡(s−1/2,  s w−3/2). \operatorname{lr}(s)=D^{-1/2}\min(s^{-1/2},\;s\,w^{-3/2}).

It's easier to picture than to read. The learning rate climbs in a straight line for the first 4,000 steps, peaks (around 0.0007 for D=512D=512 ), and then slowly decays. Small steps at the start, while things are still settling, and then a long, slow cool-down.

They also use label smoothing: instead of training towards 100% on the correct token, the target gives 10% of the probability to other tokens. Perplexity got worse with it, but accuracy and BLEU improved. The way I think about it: if the reference says "I bought a sofa", writing "couch" isn't really wrong, and plain training punishes it completely. Smoothing spreads that 10% over the whole vocabulary, though, so "couch" doesn't get any special treatment over a random word. My code uses PyTorch's built-in label_smoothing=0.1, which mixes in a uniform share: q=(1−ϵ) onehot(y)+ϵ/Vq=(1-\epsilon)\,\mathrm{onehot}(y)+\epsilon/V . Dropout shows up in two places, on each sub-layer's output before it's added back and on the embeddings plus positions. You'll see both in Phases 1 and 3.

How good were the translations? They trained on the WMT 2014 English-German and English-French datasets, with about 25,000 source and 25,000 target tokens per batch, on eight NVIDIA P100 GPUs. Translations came from beam search, keeping four candidates at each step. On English-German, Base scored 27.3 BLEU and Big scored 28.4. For English-French there's an annoying detail: the 2017 conference paper says 41.0 for Big, while a later arXiv version shows 41.8 in Table 2 but still says 41.0 in the text. So check which version you're quoting.

Did eight heads help? Their Table 3 changes one thing at a time (these are called ablations). Going from eight heads to one, at the same total width, cost 0.9 BLEU, and going up to 32 heads also made things worse. Learned positions came within 0.1 BLEU of the sinusoids. The extended paper also tried English constituency parsing, splitting sentences into phrase structure, and a four-layer model reached 91.3 F1 trained on WSJ data only. I didn't expect a translation model to do that well on a different task.

Part 3: Building it in PyTorch, phase by phase

Every phase below adds to the same file. Run the finished file with python transformer.py anywhere PyTorch is installed. It only uses ordinary tensor operations, linear layers, embeddings, dropout and LayerNorm, so you can see the attention probabilities, the head reshaping, the masks, the encoder and the decoder written out in the code. In the shape comments, L stands for either sequence length, Lq for query length, Lk for key length and F for the FFN's hidden width.

Phase 1: Embeddings and positional encoding

Think about the two copies of the in the trophy sentence. They have the same integer ID, so self.lookup returns the same row for both. Follow them through x + positions. That's the first place their vectors become different, even with dropout off. The position table only depends on length and width, so we build it once. Registering it as a buffer means PyTorch moves it along with the model when you switch devices, while the optimizer only updates the learned embeddings. 

import math

import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.nn import functional as F


class InputEmbeddings(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model):
        super().__init__()
        self.lookup = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        nn.init.normal_(self.lookup.weight, std=d_model ** -0.5)
        self.scale = math.sqrt(d_model)

    def forward(self, token_ids):
        return self.lookup(token_ids) * self.scale  # [B,L] -> [B,L,D]


class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, dropout=0.1, max_len=2048):
        super().__init__()
        pos = torch.arange(max_len, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None]  # [M,1]
        even = torch.arange(0, d_model, 2, dtype=torch.float32)  # [ceil(D/2)]
        angles = pos * torch.exp(-math.log(10000) * even / d_model)  # [M,ceil(D/2)]
        table = torch.empty(max_len, d_model)  # [M,D]
        table[:, 0::2] = angles.sin()
        table[:, 1::2] = angles[:, :d_model // 2].cos()  # Also handles odd D.
        self.register_buffer("table", table.unsqueeze(0))  # [1,M,D]
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

    def forward(self, x):
        length = x.size(1)
        if length > self.table.size(1):
            raise ValueError("Sequence exceeds max_len in PositionalEncoding")
        positions = self.table[:, :length].to(dtype=x.dtype)  # [1,L,D]
        return self.dropout(x + positions)  # [B,L,D], broadcast over batch

Phase 2: The attention function

Before reading the function, trace one cross-attention call in your head. Say the decoder has four positions and the English source has seven. Each query gets seven scores. After weights @ v, how many vectors should come out of one head?

Check the output length

Four. For one head the score matrix is 4 by 7. Its seven columns mix seven source values, once for each of the four queries. That's why scores.softmax(dim=-1) has to normalize over the last axis, which is the key axis. Normalizing down the four rows would answer a different question.

The function expects the head axis to be there already. The class under it creates that axis and then joins the heads back together. 

def scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, allowed=None):
    """True means a query may read this key. Return context and probabilities."""
    # q: [B,H,Lq,dk], k: [B,H,Lk,dk], v: [B,H,Lk,dv]
    scores = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(q.size(-1))  # [B,H,Lq,Lk]
    if allowed is not None:
        scores = scores.masked_fill(~allowed, float("-inf"))  # [B,H,Lq,Lk]
        # Softmax over all -inf is undefined. Give empty rows finite inputs,
        # then zero their probabilities below. Their returned context is zero.
        scores = scores.masked_fill(~allowed.any(dim=-1, keepdim=True), 0.0)
    weights = scores.softmax(dim=-1)  # Each query normalizes over keys.
    if allowed is not None:
        weights = weights.masked_fill(~allowed, 0.0)  # [B,H,Lq,Lk]
    return weights @ v, weights  # [B,H,Lq,dv], [B,H,Lq,Lk]


class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, heads):
        super().__init__()
        if heads < 1 or d_model % heads:
            raise ValueError("heads must be positive and divide d_model")
        self.heads = heads
        self.head_dim = d_model // heads
        self.q_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.k_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.v_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)
        self.out_proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model, bias=False)

    def split_heads(self, x):
        batch, length, _ = x.shape
        x = x.reshape(batch, length, self.heads, self.head_dim)  # [B,L,H,dk]
        return x.transpose(1, 2)  # [B,H,L,dk]

    def forward(self, queries, keys, values, allowed=None):
        q = self.split_heads(self.q_proj(queries))  # [B,H,Lq,dk]
        k = self.split_heads(self.k_proj(keys))     # [B,H,Lk,dk]
        v = self.split_heads(self.v_proj(values))   # [B,H,Lk,dv], dv=dk here
        context, _ = scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, allowed)
        context = context.transpose(1, 2)  # [B,Lq,H,dv]
        merged = context.reshape(queries.size(0), queries.size(1), -1)  # [B,Lq,D]
        return self.out_proj(merged)  # [B,Lq,D]

Each role gets one Linear(D,D), which holds all of the head-specific projection matrices packed together, so every head's projection can see every input feature. We split into heads after projecting. When you join the heads back together, transpose to [B,Lq,H,dv] before reshaping. If you reshape straight from [B,H,Lq,dv], you still get the expected output shape, but the features end up attached to the wrong tokens.

Phase 3: The sub-layers

In self.after_ff(x, self.ff(x)), follow the two arguments separately. The first is the token as it came into the sub-layer, and the second is what the FFN wants to add to it. Then read the last line of ResidualConnection from the inside of the parentheses outward to see where dropout and normalization happen. 

class PositionWiseFeedForward(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, d_ff):
        super().__init__()
        self.expand = nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff)
        self.contract = nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model)

    def forward(self, x):
        hidden = F.relu(self.expand(x))  # [B,L,D] -> [B,L,F]
        return self.contract(hidden)     # [B,L,F] -> [B,L,D]


class ResidualConnection(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, dropout):
        super().__init__()
        self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)

    def forward(self, x, update):
        # Original Post-LN order. Normalize only the final feature axis.
        return self.norm(x + self.dropout(update))  # [B,L,D]

Phase 4: Encoder and decoder blocks

Look at what each attention call receives. Passing x, x, x means all three inputs come from the same sequence, with a separate learned projection for each role. In the cross-attention call, x gives the queries and memory gives both the keys and the values. Each sub-layer has its own LayerNorm with its own learned parameters. 

class EncoderBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, heads, d_ff, dropout):
        super().__init__()
        self.self_attn = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, heads)
        self.ff = PositionWiseFeedForward(d_model, d_ff)
        self.after_attn = ResidualConnection(d_model, dropout)
        self.after_ff = ResidualConnection(d_model, dropout)

    def forward(self, x, src_allowed):
        context = self.self_attn(x, x, x, src_allowed)  # [B,S,D]
        x = self.after_attn(x, context)                 # [B,S,D]
        return self.after_ff(x, self.ff(x))             # [B,S,D]


class DecoderBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, heads, d_ff, dropout):
        super().__init__()
        self.self_attn = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, heads)
        self.cross_attn = MultiHeadAttention(d_model, heads)
        self.ff = PositionWiseFeedForward(d_model, d_ff)
        self.after_self = ResidualConnection(d_model, dropout)
        self.after_cross = ResidualConnection(d_model, dropout)
        self.after_ff = ResidualConnection(d_model, dropout)

    def forward(self, x, memory, tgt_allowed, src_allowed):
        prefix = self.self_attn(x, x, x, tgt_allowed)          # [B,T,D]
        x = self.after_self(x, prefix)                         # [B,T,D]
        source = self.cross_attn(x, memory, memory, src_allowed)  # [B,T,D]
        x = self.after_cross(x, source)                        # [B,T,D]
        return self.after_ff(x, self.ff(x))                    # [B,T,D]

Phase 5: The full Transformer and the mask helpers

The constructor builds six independent blocks in each stack by default. Since source and target share one vocabulary here, both sides use the same embedding table, and the output layer reuses that same matrix too (the paper does this as well). So the score for token j is just the decoder state dotted with token j's embedding row. The D \sqrt D scaling only applies on the input side. 

def padding_mask(ids, pad_id):
    return (ids != pad_id)[:, None, None, :]  # [B,1,1,Lk], True = real key


def causal_mask(length, device):
    allowed = torch.ones(length, length, device=device, dtype=torch.bool).tril()
    return allowed[None, None, :, :]  # [1,1,T,T], including the diagonal


class Transformer(nn.Module):
    """Shared source/target vocabulary, with a single tied embedding/output matrix."""
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model=512, heads=8, d_ff=2048,
                 layers=6, dropout=0.1, pad_id=0, max_len=2048):
        super().__init__()
        self.pad_id = pad_id
        self.embedding = InputEmbeddings(vocab_size, d_model)
        self.position = PositionalEncoding(d_model, dropout, max_len)
        self.encoders = nn.ModuleList(
            EncoderBlock(d_model, heads, d_ff, dropout) for _ in range(layers)
        )
        self.decoders = nn.ModuleList(
            DecoderBlock(d_model, heads, d_ff, dropout) for _ in range(layers)
        )
        self.projection = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.projection.weight = self.embedding.lookup.weight  # same Parameter [V,D]

    def encode(self, src_ids, src_allowed):
        memory = self.position(self.embedding(src_ids))  # [B,S,D]
        for block in self.encoders:
            memory = block(memory, src_allowed)          # [B,S,D]
        return memory

    def decode(self, tgt_in, memory, src_allowed):
        real_keys = padding_mask(tgt_in, self.pad_id)              # [B,1,1,T]
        earlier = causal_mask(tgt_in.size(1), tgt_in.device)       # [1,1,T,T]
        tgt_allowed = real_keys & earlier                          # [B,1,T,T]
        x = self.position(self.embedding(tgt_in))                  # [B,T,D]
        for block in self.decoders:
            x = block(x, memory, tgt_allowed, src_allowed)         # [B,T,D]
        return self.projection(x)                                  # [B,T,V] logits

    def forward(self, src_ids, tgt_in):
        src_allowed = padding_mask(src_ids, self.pad_id)  # [B,1,1,S]
        memory = self.encode(src_ids, src_allowed)        # [B,S,D]
        return self.decode(tgt_in, memory, src_allowed)   # [B,T,V]

The model returns raw logits, and PyTorch's cross-entropy applies log-softmax for you. To generate a translation, encode the source once, start tgt_in with BOS, decode, and pick a token from logits[:, -1, :]. Append that token and repeat until you get EOS or hit a length limit. The training example below can compute all the rows at once because every prediction already has a known prefix.

Phase 6: Checking the forward and backward passes

Try to think of a way to break this model that print(logits.shape) wouldn't catch. Suppose you replace real_keys & earlier in Phase 5 with just real_keys. The output still has one row per decoder position and one column per vocabulary entry. Which assertion below should fail first?

Find the test that catches the leak

The first assert_close. It compares the prefix predictions before and after changing a later target token. Without earlier, positions 0 and 1 can read position 2, so changing that token can move their predictions. The shape and finiteness checks still pass. This is also why net.eval() matters here: with dropout on, even two identical inputs can give different results.

The second comparison adds extra source padding. After that we switch back to training mode and check that the loss sends a finite, nonzero gradient back to the first encoder layer. 

def sanity_check():
    torch.manual_seed(7)
    # Same topology, smaller dimensions so the example runs quickly.
    net = Transformer(vocab_size=32, d_model=32, heads=4, d_ff=64, layers=2)
    src = torch.tensor([[4, 5, 6, 2, 0], [7, 8, 2, 0, 0]])  # [2,5]
    # 0=PAD, 1=BOS, 2=EOS. Shift before feeding the decoder.
    tgt = torch.tensor([[1, 9, 10, 11, 2], [1, 12, 2, 0, 0]])  # [2,5]
    tgt_in, labels = tgt[:, :-1], tgt[:, 1:]                   # both [2,4]

    net.eval()  # Disable dropout so differences reveal mask failures.
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = net(src, tgt_in)  # [2,4,32]
        assert logits.shape == (2, 4, 32)
        assert torch.isfinite(logits).all()

        # Edit position 2. Predictions at positions 0 and 1 must be unchanged.
        edited = tgt_in.clone()
        edited[0, 2] = 15
        torch.testing.assert_close(net(src, edited)[:, :2], logits[:, :2])

        # Extra source padding should contribute nothing in either attention path.
        padded = F.pad(src, (0, 2), value=net.pad_id)  # [2,7]
        torch.testing.assert_close(net(padded, tgt_in), logits, atol=1e-5, rtol=1e-5)

    net.train()
    train_logits = net(src, tgt_in)  # [2,4,32]
    loss = F.cross_entropy(train_logits.flatten(0, 1), labels.reshape(-1),
                           ignore_index=net.pad_id, label_smoothing=0.1)  # scalar
    loss.backward()
    grad = net.encoders[0].self_attn.q_proj.weight.grad
    assert grad is not None and torch.isfinite(grad).all() and grad.abs().sum() > 0
    print("source", tuple(src.shape), "decoder input", tuple(tgt_in.shape))
    print("logits", tuple(logits.shape), "labels", tuple(labels.shape))
    print("PASS: causal mask, source padding, backward pass")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sanity_check()

When you run it, you should see: 

source (2, 5) decoder input (2, 4)
logits (2, 4, 32) labels (2, 4)
PASS: causal mask, source padding, backward pass

Look at logits[0, 1] from that example. It's a vector of 32 scores. For the first sentence, the decoder has seen token IDs 1 and 9, and the reference says the next ID is 10, so the loss rewards putting probability on entry 10 of that vector. That one lookup connects the model's output back to the shifted-label table in Part 2. Passing these checks means information flows correctly through the paths we tested. Getting the model to translate would take many updates on real sentence pairs.

Part 4: Summary and what came after

The original Base and Big configurations

Setting Base Big
Encoder blocks / decoder blocks 6 / 6 6 / 6
Model width D 512 1,024
FFN hidden width 2,048 4,096
Heads per attention sub-layer 8 16
Per-head key / value width 64 / 64 64 / 64
Dropout, English-German 0.1 0.3
Label smoothing 0.1 0.1
Warmup steps 4,000 4,000
Training steps 100,000 300,000
Approximate parameters, paper configurations 65 million 213 million
Reported training time on eight P100s 12 hours 3.5 days

Big keeps the per-head width the same and just adds more of everything. The English-French Big run used dropout 0.1 instead of 0.3. If you change the vocabulary size in my example, the parameter count changes too, since the embedding table is a big chunk of it.

From translation to GPT and BERT

Family Which information can a token read? What is it trained to predict?
Original encoder-decoder Transformer The encoder sees the complete source. The decoder sees its target prefix and the source memory. Supervised translation: the next target token, given both.
GPT-style decoder-only Transformer A causal stack reads the prefix of one sequence. The prompt and the continuation share that sequence. The next token. Without a separate encoder, the decoder also loses its source cross-attention sub-layer.
BERT-style encoder-only Transformer Bidirectional self-attention reads a given, partly corrupted sequence from both sides. The original tokens at selected positions. The original BERT also had a next-sentence prediction objective.

The suitcase sentence works for all three. Give a GPT-style model "The trophy doesn't fit into the" and it can predict a sensible continuation from that prefix. Give BERT "The trophy doesn't fit into the [MASK] because it's too small" and it can use the words after the gap as evidence. Give the original translation model the full English sentence, and it can look at the final English adjective while choosing the French pronoun halfway through its translation.

One experiment I'd try before closing the tab: run the script once, then change real_keys & earlier to real_keys so the decoder can read future words, and run it again. The tensor still has shape [2,4,32], but the prefix check fails, and putting the mask back makes it pass again. That & earlier is the line of Python I mentioned at the start, the one that keeps the next French word hidden during training.

oneSentenceSummary: 本文分阶段全面拆解《注意力就是一切》论文，并提供详细的 PyTorch 实现指导，适合熟悉 Python 但初次接触研究论文的读者。
summary: 本文面向熟悉 Python、但初次接触学术论文的读者，详细讲解了具有开创意义的《注意力就是一切》。文章从 Winograd 模式等直观例子入手，说明为何需要注意力机制。随后，作者系统拆解 Transformer 架构：张量形状、点积与 softmax、关键 PyTorch 组件（nn.Module、nn.Linear、nn.LayerNorm、nn.Dropout），以及 RNN 速度较慢的原因。文章还通过注意力环节（编码器自注意力、解码器自注意力、交叉注意力）、使用正弦和余弦函数进行位置编码的嵌入、带有 sqrt(dk) 缩放因子的缩放点积注意力、包含 8 个头的多头注意力，以及掩码技术（填充掩码和因果掩码），解释论文中的架构。文中还提供实用的 PyTorch 代码片段，旨在帮助读者亲自实现该模型。

mainPoints.point: 文章通过直观示例和实用的 PyTorch 代码讲解 Transformer 架构。
mainPoints.explanation: 文章使用 Winograd 模式说明注意力机制如何消解歧义，随后拆解编码器—解码器结构、注意力机制，以及 nn.Linear 和 nn.LayerNorm 等关键 PyTorch 组件。

mainPoints.point: 缩放点积注意力使用 sqrt(dk) 进行缩放，避免 softmax 变得过度自信。
mainPoints.explanation: 如果不进行缩放，64 个特征的点积方差将达到 64，导致 softmax 几乎把所有权重都分配给得分最高的项，使学习受阻。除以 sqrt(dk) 可以将得分控制在适当范围内，让 softmax 的梯度仍能提供有效信息。

mainPoints.point: 多头注意力让不同的表示子空间能够关注输入的不同部分。
mainPoints.explanation: 使用 8 个头时，每个头会将 512 个特征投影到 64 维，使模型能够同时关注不同方面（例如名词与形容词）；最后通过一个线性层，将拼接后的各个头混合回 512 维。

mainPoints.point: 位置编码使用不同频率的正弦和余弦函数来表示词元的位置。
mainPoints.explanation: 这种方法让模型能够学习相对位置，因为位置 p+k 的编码可以表示为位置 p 编码的线性函数；此外，正弦波还可能帮助模型泛化到比训练时更长的序列。

mainPoints.point: 掩码技术可以防止解码器关注填充词元和未来词元。
mainPoints.explanation: 填充掩码可确保 PAD 词元不会稀释注意力权重；因果掩码（上三角矩阵）则确保解码器的每个位置只能关注此前的位置，避免泄露未来词元的信息。

keyQuotes: 「如果你写过游戏循环，就写过世界模型：状态 → 动作 → 下一状态 → 渲染。」
「Softmax 会把一组分数转换成总和为 1 的份额：对每个分数取 e 的幂，再除以总和。」
「第一行里唯一看起来奇怪的数字，就是 dk 除以 sqrt(dk)。」
「Transformer 不会只选一行，而是对所有行进行加权混合。」
